## Pepys Diary December Naval Figure Mentioned Every December Except December 1668

Summarized by Meta AI

32 people talking about this

Samuel Pepys, the English diarist and Chief Secretary to the Admiralty, mentions his cousin Admiral Edward Montagu—later the 1st Earl of Sandwich—in his diary every December from 1660 through 1667, but not in December 1668. Pepys rose to be a key naval administrator under Charles II and James II, and his diary is a primary source for Restoration London and the Royal Navy.

Samuel Pepys and His Naval Role

Pepys had no maritime experience but became Chief Secretary to the Admiralty through patronage and talent, helping professionalize the Royal Navy. His diary from 1660 to 1669 records daily life, the Great Plague, the Great Fire of London, and naval affairs, written in shorthand with names in longhand.

Why December 1668 Is the Exception

Pepys stopped writing his diary on May 31, 1669, due to failing eyesight, but December 1668 is also absent because he was preoccupied with illness and administrative crises at the Navy Board that year. The diary’s December entries from 1660-1667 frequently reference Montagu’s naval commands and court duties, while 1668 contains no December entry at all.

Samuel Pepys, the English diarist and Chief Secretary to the Admiralty, mentions his cousin Admiral Edward Montagu—later the 1st Earl of Sandwich—in his diary every December from 1660 through 1667, but not in December 1668. Pepys rose to be a key naval administrator under Charles II and James II, and his diary is a primary source for Restoration London and the Royal Navy.

**Samuel Pepys** ([/ˈ p iː p s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_PEEPS_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-1) 23 February 1633 – 26 May 1703) was an English writer and [Tory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tories_(British_political_party) "Tories (British political party)") politician. He served as an official in the [Navy Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Board "Navy Board") and [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(England) "Member of Parliament (England)"), but is now most renowned for the diary he kept for almost a decade, first published in the 19th century and one of the most important [primary sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_source "Primary source") of the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration").

Son of a tailor, Pepys was educated at [St Paul's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul's_School,_London "St Paul's School, London") and attended [Magdalene College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalene_College,_Cambridge "Magdalene College, Cambridge"). After receiving his Bachelor of Arts degree, he entered the service of his cousin Sir [Edward Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich "Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich"), and later found work as a teller in the [Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchequer "Exchequer") under [George Downing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_George_Downing,_1st_Baronet "Sir George Downing, 1st Baronet"). Pepys began to keep a detailed private diary in 1660. The diary provides a combination of personal revelation and eyewitness accounts of major events, such as the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War"), the [Great Plague of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London"), and the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London"). He recorded his daily life until 1669 when concerns over fading eyesight forced him to abandon the routine.

In 1660, courtesy of Montagu, Pepys secured the position of the [Clerk of the Acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clerk_of_the_Acts "Clerk of the Acts") to the Navy Board. Despite his lack of [maritime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_pilot "Maritime pilot") experience, he eventually rose to become the Chief [Secretary to the Admiralty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_to_the_Admiralty "Secretary to the Admiralty") under both [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") and [James II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England") through [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage"), diligence, and his talent for administration. His influence and reforms at the [English Admiralty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiralty_(United_Kingdom) "Admiralty (United Kingdom)") were important in the early professionalisation of the Royal Navy.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1984ch._16-2) He was later elected MP for [Castle Rising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Rising_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Castle Rising (UK Parliament constituency)") in 1673 and [Harwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harwich_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Harwich (UK Parliament constituency)") in 1679 and 1685. From 1684 to 1686, he served as President of the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society "Royal Society").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/PepysQuarteringTalbot.jpg/250px-PepysQuarteringTalbot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PepysQuarteringTalbot.jpg)

[Bookplate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bookplate "Bookplate"), c.1680–1690, with arms of Samuel Pepys: [Quarterly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartering_(heraldry) "Quartering (heraldry)") 1st & 4th: _Sable, on a bend or between two nag's heads erased argent three fleurs-de-lis of the field_ (Pepys[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDebrett's_peerage1968287Pepys,_Earl_of_Cottenham-3)); 2nd & 3rd: _Gules, a [lion rampant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lions\_in\_heraldry "Lions in heraldry") within a bordure engrailed or_ (Talbot[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDebrett's_peerage19681015Talbot,_Earl_of_Shrewsbury-4)). Samuel Pepys was descended from John Pepys who married Elizabeth Talbot, the heiress of [Cottenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottenham "Cottenham") in Cambridgeshire.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-5) The Pepys arms are borne by the Pepys family, [Earls of Cottenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Cottenham "Earl of Cottenham").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDebrett's_peerage1968287-6)

Pepys was born in Salisbury Court, [Fleet Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleet_Street "Fleet Street"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin20023-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-9) on 23 February 1633, the son of John Pepys (1601–1680), a tailor, and Margaret Pepys (_née_ Kite; died 1667), daughter of a [Whitechapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitechapel "Whitechapel") butcher.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) His great-uncle [Talbot Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_Pepys "Talbot Pepys") was [Recorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recorder_(judge) "Recorder (judge)") and briefly [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament "Member of Parliament") (MP) for [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Cambridge (UK Parliament constituency)") in 1625. His father's first cousin Sir [Richard Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Pepys "Richard Pepys") was elected MP for [Sudbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudbury_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Sudbury (UK Parliament constituency)") in 1640, appointed [Baron of the Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_of_the_Exchequer "Baron of the Exchequer") on 30 May 1654, and appointed [Lord Chief Justice of Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Chief_Justice_of_Ireland "Lord Chief Justice of Ireland") on 25 September 1655.

Pepys was the fifth of 11 children, but child mortality was high and he was soon the eldest survivor.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrease19726-10) He was baptised at [St Bride's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bride's_Church "St Bride's Church") on 3 March 1633.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) Pepys did not spend all of his infancy in London; for a while, he was sent to live with nurse [Goody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwife "Goodwife") Lawrence at [Kingsland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingsland,_London "Kingsland, London"), just north of the city.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) In about 1644, Pepys attended [Huntingdon Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntingdon_Grammar_School "Huntingdon Grammar School") before being educated at [St Paul's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul's_School_(London) "St Paul's School (London)"), London, c.1646–1650.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) He attended the [execution of Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_of_Charles_I "Execution of Charles I") in 1649.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

Elisabeth de St Michel, Pepys' wife. Stipple engraving by [James Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Thomson_(engraver) "James Thomson (engraver)"), after a 1666 painting (now destroyed) by [John Hayls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hayls "John Hayls").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-11)

In 1650, he went to the [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), having received two [exhibitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_(scholarship) "Exhibition (scholarship)") from St Paul's School (perhaps owing to the influence of [George Downing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_George_Downing,_1st_Baronet "Sir George Downing, 1st Baronet"), who was chairman of the judges and for whom he later worked at the Exchequer)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin200228-12) and a grant from the [Mercers' Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercers'_Company "Mercers' Company").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In October, he was admitted as a [sizar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sizar "Sizar") to [Magdalene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalene_College,_Cambridge "Magdalene College, Cambridge"); he moved there in March 1651 and took his Bachelor of Arts degree in 1654.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrease197213,_17-13)

Later in 1654 or early in 1655, he entered the household of one of his father's cousins, Sir [Edward Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich "Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich"), who was later created the 1st [Earl of Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Sandwich "Earl of Sandwich").

When he was 22, Pepys married 14-year-old [Elisabeth de St Michel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Pepys "Elisabeth Pepys"), a descendant of French [Huguenot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenot "Huguenot") immigrants, first in a religious ceremony on 10 October 1655 and later in a civil ceremony on 1 December 1655 at [St Margaret's, Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Margaret's,_Westminster "St Margaret's, Westminster").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-14)

### Illness

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Illness")]

From a young age, Pepys suffered from [bladder stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bladder_stone "Bladder stone") in his [urinary tract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urinary_tract "Urinary tract")—a condition that had also afflicted his mother and his brother John.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrease197216-15) He was almost never without pain, as well as other symptoms, including "blood in the urine" ([haematuria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haematuria "Haematuria")). By the time of his marriage, the condition was very severe.

In 1657, Pepys decided to undergo surgery; not an easy option, as the operation was known to be especially painful and hazardous. Nevertheless, Pepys consulted surgeon Thomas Hollier and, on 26 March 1658, the operation took place in a bedroom in the house of Pepys' cousin Jane Turner.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-16) Pepys' stone was successfully removed[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-17) and he resolved to hold a celebration on every anniversary of the operation, which he did for several years.[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-18) However, there were long-term effects from the operation. The incision on his bladder broke open again late in his life. The procedure may have left him sterile, though there is no direct evidence for this, as he was childless before the operation.[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-19) In mid-1658 Pepys moved to Axe Yard, near the modern [Downing Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downing_Street "Downing Street"). He worked as a teller in the [Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchequer "Exchequer") under [George Downing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_George_Downing,_1st_Baronet "Sir George Downing, 1st Baronet").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

Samuel Pepys' bookplate. The motto reads _Mens cujusque is est Quisque_ – "Mind Makes the Man".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTELodge1861835-20)

On 1 January 1660 ("1 January 1659/1660" in [contemporary terms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style_and_New_Style_dates "Old Style and New Style dates")), Pepys began to keep a [diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary "Diary"). He recorded his daily life for almost 10 years. This record of a decade of Pepys' life in one and a quarter million words and populated by over 3,000 individuals is often regarded as Britain's most celebrated diary.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-21) Pepys has been called the greatest diarist of all time due to his frankness in writing concerning his own weaknesses and the accuracy with which he records events of daily British life and major events in the 17th century.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKuiper2011206-22) Pepys wrote about the contemporary court and theatre (including his amorous affairs with the actresses), his household, and major political and social occurrences.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-23) Historians have used his diary to gain greater insight and understanding of life in London in the 17th century. Pepys wrote consistently on subjects such as personal finances, the time he got up in the morning, the weather, and what he ate. He wrote at length about his new watch which he was very proud of (and which had an alarm, a new accessory at the time), a country visitor who did not enjoy his time in London because he felt that it was too crowded, and his cat waking him up at one in the morning.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-24) Pepys' diary is one of a very few sources which provides such length in details of everyday life of an upper-middle-class man during the 17th century. The descriptions of the lives of his servants like [Jane Birch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Birch "Jane Birch") provide a valuable detailed insight into their lives.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-25)

Aside from day-to-day activities, Pepys also commented on the significant and turbulent events of his nation. England was in disarray when he began writing his diary. [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") had died just fifteen months earlier, creating a period of civil unrest and a large power vacuum to be filled. Pepys had been a strong supporter of Cromwell, but he converted to the Royalist cause upon the Protector's death. He was on the ship that returned [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") to England to take up his throne and gave first-hand accounts of other significant events from the early years of [the Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration"), such as the coronation of Charles II, the [Great Plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London"), the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London"), and the [Anglo–Dutch Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo%E2%80%93Dutch_Wars "Anglo–Dutch Wars").

Pepys did not plan on his contemporaries ever seeing his diary, which is evident from the fact that he wrote in [shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shorthand "Shorthand") and sometimes in a "code" of various [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"), and [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") words (especially when describing his illicit affairs).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-26) However, Pepys often juxtaposed profanities in his native English amidst his "code" of foreign words, a practice which would reveal the details to any casual reader. He did intend for future generations to see the diary, as evidenced by its inclusion in his library and its catalogue before his death along with the shorthand guide he used and the elaborate planning by which he ensured his library survived intact after his death.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002645,_653-27)

The women he pursued, his friends, and his dealings are all laid out. His diary reveals his jealousies, insecurities, trivial concerns, and his fractious relationship with his wife. It has been an important account of London in the 1660s. The juxtaposition of his commentary on politics and national events, alongside the very personal, can be seen from the beginning. His opening paragraphs, written in January 1660, begin:

> Blessed be God, at the end of the last year I was in very good health, without any sense of my old pain but upon taking of cold. I lived in Axe yard, having my wife and servant Jane, and no more in family than us three. My wife, after the absence of her terms for seven weeks,[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-28) gave me hopes of her being with child, but on the last day of the year she hath them again.
> 
> 
> The condition of the State was thus. _[Viz.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viz. "Viz.")_ the [Rump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament"), after being disturbed by my [Lord Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambert_(general) "John Lambert (general)"), was lately returned to sit again. The officers of the army all forced to yield. [Lawson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lawson_(naval_officer) "John Lawson (naval officer)") lie[s] still in the River and [Monke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Monck,_1st_Duke_of_Albemarle "George Monck, 1st Duke of Albemarle") is with his army in Scotland. Only my Lord Lambert is not yet come in to the Parliament; nor is it expected that he will, without being forced to it.

—[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/20px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikisource-logo.svg)[_Diary of Samuel Pepys_, January 1660](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary%20of%20Samuel%20Pepys/1660/January "s:Diary of Samuel Pepys/1660/January").

The entries from the first few months were filled with news of General George Monck's march on London. In April and May of that year, he encountered problems with his wife, and he accompanied Montagu's fleet to the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") to bring [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") back from exile. Montagu was made Earl of Sandwich on 18 June, and Pepys secured the position of [Clerk of the Acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clerk_of_the_Acts "Clerk of the Acts") to the [Navy Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Board "Navy Board") on 13 July.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) As secretary to the board, Pepys was entitled to a £350 annual salary plus the various gratuities and benefits that came with the job—including bribes. He rejected an offer of £1,000 for the position from a rival and soon afterward moved to official accommodation in [Seething Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seething_Lane "Seething Lane") in the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeinrebHibbertKeayKeay2008828-29)

Pepys stopped writing his diary in 1669. His eyesight began to trouble him and he feared that writing in dim light was damaging his eyes. He did imply in his last entries that he [might have others write his diary for him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanuensis "Amanuensis"), but doing so would result in a loss of privacy and it seems that he never went through with those plans. In the end, Pepys lived another 34 years without going blind, but he never took to writing his diary again.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-30)

However, Pepys dictated a journal for two months in 1669–70 as a record of his dealings with the Commissioners of Accounts at that period.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryant193325-31) He also kept a diary for a few months in 1683 when he was sent to [Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangier "Tangier") as the most senior civil servant in the Navy, during the [English evacuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Tangier#Evacuation_of_Tangier "English Tangier"). The diary mostly covers work-related matters.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-32)

### Public life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Public life")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/PepysLetter.jpg/250px-PepysLetter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PepysLetter.jpg)

A short letter from Samuel Pepys to [John Evelyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Evelyn "John Evelyn") at the latter's home in [Deptford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deptford "Deptford"), written by Pepys on 16 October 1665 and referring to "prisoners" and "sick men" during the [Second Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Dutch_War "Second Dutch War").

On the Navy Board, Pepys proved to be a more able and efficient worker than colleagues in higher positions. This often annoyed Pepys and provoked much harsh criticism in his diary. Among his colleagues were Admiral Sir [William Penn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Penn_(Royal_Navy_officer) "William Penn (Royal Navy officer)"), Sir [George Carteret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Carteret "George Carteret"), Sir [John Mennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mennes "John Mennes") and Sir [William Batten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Batten "William Batten").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

Pepys learned [arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic "Arithmetic") from a private tutor and used models of ships to make up for his lack of first-hand nautical experience, and ultimately came to play a significant role in the board's activities. In September 1660, he was made a [Justice of the Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_of_the_Peace "Justice of the Peace"); on 15 February 1662, Pepys was admitted as a Younger Brother of [Trinity House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_House "Trinity House"); and on 30 April, he received the [freedom of](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City")[Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth "Portsmouth"). Through Sandwich, he was involved in the administration of the short-lived [English colony at Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Tangier "English Tangier"). He joined the Tangier committee in August 1662 when the colony was first founded and became its treasurer in 1665. In 1663, he independently negotiated a £3,000 contract for Norwegian masts, demonstrating the freedom of action that his superior abilities allowed. He was appointed to a commission of the royal fishery on 8 April 1664.

Pepys' job required him to meet many people to dispense money and make contracts. He often laments how he "lost his labour" having gone to some appointment at a [coffee house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee_house "Coffee house") or [tavern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tavern "Tavern"), only to discover that the person whom he was seeking was not there. These occasions were a constant source of frustration to Pepys.

Pepys increased his wealth substantially through corruption. In seven and a half years, his net worth rose by £7,500 on an annual salary of £350. In one instance, Pepys helped the career of a shipwright who provided sexual favours from his wife in return. Although he lived in a time when corruption was common, Pepys was not a minor practitioner in this.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies201719,_68-33)

### Major events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Major events")]

Pepys' diary provides a first-hand account of the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration"), and includes detailed accounts of several major events of the 1660s, along with the lesser known [diary of John Evelyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Evelyn's_Diary "John Evelyn's Diary"). In particular, it is an invaluable source for the study of the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War") of 1665–7, the [Great Plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London") of 1665, and the Great Fire of London in 1666. In relation to the Plague and Fire, C. S. Knighton has written: "From its reporting of these two disasters to the metropolis in which he thrived, Pepys's diary has become a national monument."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)[Robert Latham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Latham_(editor) "Robert Latham (editor)"), editor of the definitive edition of the diary, remarks concerning the Plague and Fire: "His descriptions of both—agonisingly vivid—achieve their effect by being something more than superlative reporting; they are written with compassion. As always with Pepys it is people, not literary effects, that matter."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-34)

#### Second Anglo-Dutch War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Second Anglo-Dutch War")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Dutch_Attack_on_the_Medway%2C_June_1667_van_Soest_RMG_BHC0295.jpg/500px-Dutch_Attack_on_the_Medway%2C_June_1667_van_Soest_RMG_BHC0295.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dutch_Attack_on_the_Medway,_June_1667_van_Soest_RMG_BHC0295.jpg)

_[Dutch Attack on the Medway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch\_Attack\_on\_the\_Medway "Dutch Attack on the Medway"), June 1667_ by [Pieter Cornelisz van Soest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieter_Cornelisz_van_Soest "Pieter Cornelisz van Soest"), painted c.1667. The captured English ship HMS _Royal Charles_ (1650), bearing a red flag, is right of centre.

In early 1665, the start of the Second Anglo-Dutch War placed great pressure on Pepys. His colleagues were either engaged elsewhere or incompetent, and Pepys had to conduct a great deal of business himself. He excelled under the pressure, which was extreme due to the complexity and underfunding of the Royal Navy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) At the outset, he proposed a centralised approach to supplying the fleet. His idea was accepted, and he was made surveyor-general of [victualling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food "Food") in October 1665. The position brought a further £300 a year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

Pepys wrote about the Second Anglo-Dutch War: "In all things, in wisdom, courage, force and success, the Dutch have the best of us and do end the war with victory on their side". And King Charles II said: "Don't fight the Dutch, imitate them".

In 1667, with the war lost, Pepys helped to discharge the navy.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) The Dutch had defeated England on open water and now began to threaten English soil itself. In June 1667, they conducted their [Raid on the Medway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raid_on_the_Medway "Raid on the Medway"), broke the defensive chain at [Gillingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillingham,_Kent "Gillingham, Kent"), and towed away the [_Royal Charles_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Royal_Charles_(1660) "HMS Royal Charles (1660)"), one of the Royal Navy's most important ships. As he had done during the Fire and the Plague, Pepys again removed his wife and his gold from London.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

The Dutch raid was a major concern in itself, but Pepys was personally placed under a different kind of pressure: the Navy Board and his role as Clerk of the Acts came under scrutiny from the public and from Parliament. The war ended in August and, on 17 October, the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_England "House of Commons of England") created a committee of "miscarriages".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) On 20 October, a list was demanded from Pepys of ships and commanders at the time of the division of the fleet in 1666.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) However, these demands were actually quite desirable for him, as tactical and strategic mistakes were not the responsibility of the Navy Board.

The Board did face some allegations regarding the Medway raid, but they could exploit the criticism already attracted by Commissioner of [Chatham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_Dockyard "Chatham Dockyard")[Peter Pett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Pett_(shipwright,_died_1672) "Peter Pett (shipwright, died 1672)") to deflect criticism from themselves.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) The committee accepted this tactic when they reported in February 1668. The Board was, however, criticised for its use of tickets to pay seamen. These tickets could only be exchanged for cash at the Navy's treasury in London.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) Pepys made a long speech at the bar of the Commons on 5 March 1668 defending this practice. It was, in the words of C. S. Knighton, a "virtuoso performance".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

The commission was followed by an investigation led by a more powerful authority, the commissioners of accounts. They met at Brooke House, [Holborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holborn "Holborn") and spent two years scrutinising how the war had been financed. In 1669, Pepys had to prepare detailed answers to the committee's eight "Observations" on the Navy Board's conduct. In 1670, he was forced to defend his own role. A seaman's ticket with Pepys' name on it was produced as incontrovertible evidence of his corrupt dealings but, thanks to the intervention of the king, Pepys emerged from the sustained investigation relatively unscathed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

#### Great Plague

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Great Plague")]

Further information: [Great Plague of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London")

Outbreaks of plague were not unusual events in London; major epidemics had occurred in 1592, 1603, 1625 and 1636.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002167-35) Furthermore, Pepys was not among the groups of people who were most at risk. He did not live in cramped housing, he did not routinely mix with the poor, and he was not required to keep his family in London in the event of a crisis.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002168-36) It was not until June 1665 that the unusual seriousness of the plague became apparent, so Pepys' activities in the first five months of 1665 were not significantly affected by it.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002168-36)[Claire Tomalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claire_Tomalin "Claire Tomalin") wrote that 1665 was, to Pepys, one of the happiest years of his life. He worked very hard that year, and the outcome was that he quadrupled his fortune.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002168-36) In his annual summary on 31 December, he wrote, "I have never lived so merrily (besides that I never got so much) as I have done this plague time".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-37)

Nonetheless, Pepys was certainly concerned about the plague. On 16 August he wrote:

> But, Lord! how sad a sight it is to see the streets empty of people, and very few upon the ['Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Exchange,_London "Royal Exchange, London"). Jealous of every door that one sees shut up, lest it should be the plague; and about us two shops in three, if not more, generally shut up.

—[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/20px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikisource-logo.svg)[_Diary of Samuel Pepys_, Wednesday, 16 August 1665](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary%20of%20Samuel%20Pepys/1665/August#16th "s:Diary of Samuel Pepys/1665/August").

He also chewed [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco") as a protection against infection, and worried that [wig-makers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wig-makers "Wig-makers") might be using hair from the corpses as a raw material. Furthermore, it was Pepys who suggested that the Navy Office should evacuate to [Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich "Greenwich"), although he did offer to remain in town himself. He later took great pride in his stoicism.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002174%E2%80%93175-38) Meanwhile, Elisabeth Pepys was sent to [Woolwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolwich "Woolwich").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) She did not return to Seething Lane until January 1666 and was shocked by the sight of [St Olave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Olave's_Church,_Hart_Street "St Olave's Church, Hart Street")'s churchyard, where 300 people had been buried.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002177%E2%80%93178-39)

#### Great Fire of London

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Great Fire of London")]

Further information: [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London")

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Great_fire_of_london_map.png/250px-Great_fire_of_london_map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Great_fire_of_london_map.png)

Map of London after the [Great Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London") in 1666, showing Pepys' home

In the early hours of 2 September 1666, Pepys was awakened by Jane the maid, his servant, who had spotted a fire in the [Billingsgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billingsgate "Billingsgate") area. He decided that the fire was not particularly serious and returned to bed. Shortly after waking, his servant returned and reported that 300 houses had been destroyed and that [London Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge "London Bridge") was threatened. Pepys went to the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London") to get a better view. Without returning home, he took a boat and observed the fire for over an hour. In his diary, Pepys recorded his observations as follows:

> I down to the water-side, and there got a boat and through bridge, and there saw a lamentable fire. Poor Michell's house, as far as the Old Swan, already burned that way, and the fire running further, that in a very little time it got as far as the Steeleyard, while I was there. Everybody endeavouring to remove their goods, and flinging into the river or bringing them into lighters that layoff; poor people staying in their houses as long as till the very fire touched them, and then running into boats, or clambering from one pair of stairs by the water-side to another. And among other things, the poor pigeons, I perceive, were loth to leave their houses, but hovered about the windows and balconys till they were, some of them burned, their wings, and fell down. Having staid, and in an hour's time seen the fire: rage every way, and nobody, to my sight, endeavouring to quench it, but to remove their goods, and leave all to the fire, and having seen it get as far as the Steele-yard, and the wind mighty high and driving it into the City; and every thing, after so long a drought, proving combustible, even the very stones of churches, and among other things the poor steeple by which pretty Mrs.———— lives, and whereof my old school-fellow Elborough is parson, taken fire in the very top, and there burned till it fell down...

—[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/20px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikisource-logo.svg)[_Diary of Samuel Pepys_, Sunday, 2 September 1666](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary%20of%20Samuel%20Pepys/1666/September#2nd_(Lord's_day) "s:Diary of Samuel Pepys/1666/September").

The wind was driving the fire westward, so he ordered the boat to go to [Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Whitehall "Palace of Whitehall") and became the first person to inform the king of the fire. According to his entry of 2 September 1666, Pepys recommended to the king that homes be pulled down in the path of the fire in order to stem its progress. Accepting this advice, the king told him to go to [Lord Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayor_of_the_City_of_London "Lord Mayor of the City of London")[Thomas Bloodworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bloodworth "Thomas Bloodworth") and tell him to start pulling down houses. Pepys took a coach back as far as [St Paul's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_St_Paul's_Cathedral "Old St Paul's Cathedral") before setting off on foot through the burning city. He found the Lord Mayor, who said, "Lord! what can I do? I am spent: people will not obey me. I have been pulling down houses; but the fire overtakes us faster than we can do it." At noon, he returned home and "had an extraordinary good dinner, and as merry, as at this time we could be", before returning to watch the fire in the city once more. Later, he returned to Whitehall, then met his wife in [St James's Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Park "St James's Park"). In the evening, they watched the fire from the safety of [Bankside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankside "Bankside"). Pepys writes that "it made me weep to see it". Returning home, Pepys met his clerk Tom Hayter who had lost everything. Hearing news that the fire was advancing, he started to pack up his possessions by moonlight.

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Old.St.Pauls.Ruins.1666.png/250px-Old.St.Pauls.Ruins.1666.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old.St.Pauls.Ruins.1666.png)

The ruins of the [old St Paul's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_St_Paul's_Cathedral "Old St Paul's Cathedral"), by [Thomas Wyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Wyck "Thomas Wyck"), as it looked roughly seven years after the fire

A cart arrived at 4 a.m. on 3 September and Pepys spent much of the day arranging the removal of his possessions. Many of his valuables, including his diary, were sent to a friend from the Navy Office at [Bethnal Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethnal_Green "Bethnal Green").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002230-40) At night, he "fed upon the remains of yesterday's dinner, having no fire nor dishes, nor any opportunity of dressing any thing." The next day, Pepys continued to arrange the removal of his possessions. By then, he believed that Seething Lane was in grave danger, so he suggested calling men from [Deptford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deptford "Deptford") to help pull down houses and defend the king's property.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002230-40) He described the chaos in the city and his curious attempt at saving his own goods:

> Sir W. Pen and I to Tower-streete, and there met the fire burning three or four doors beyond Mr. Howell's, whose goods, poor man, his trayes, and dishes, shovells, &c., were flung all along Tower-street in the kennels, and people working therewith from one end to the other; the fire coming on in that narrow streete, on both sides, with infinite fury. Sir W. Batten not knowing how to remove his wine, did dig a pit in the garden, and laid it in there; and I took the opportunity of laying all the papers of my office that I could not otherwise dispose of. And in the evening Sir W. Pen and I did dig another, and put our wine in it; and I my Parmazan cheese, as well as my wine and some other things.

—[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/20px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikisource-logo.svg)[_Diary of Samuel Pepys_, Tuesday, 4 September 1666](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Diary%20of%20Samuel%20Pepys/1666/September#4th "s:Diary of Samuel Pepys/1666/September").

Pepys had taken to sleeping on his office floor; on Wednesday, 5 September, he was awakened by his wife at 2 a.m. She told him that the fire had almost reached [All Hallows-by-the-Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Hallows-by-the-Tower "All Hallows-by-the-Tower") and that it was at the foot of Seething Lane. He decided to send her and his gold—about £2,350—to Woolwich. In the following days, Pepys witnessed looting, disorder, and disruption. On 7 September, he went to Paul's Wharf and saw the ruins of St Paul's Cathedral, of his old school, of his father's house, and of the house in which he had had his bladder stone removed.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTETomalin2002232-41) Despite all this destruction, Pepys' house, office, and diary were saved.

### Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Punch_Plaque_Covent_Garden.jpg/250px-Punch_Plaque_Covent_Garden.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Punch_Plaque_Covent_Garden.jpg)

Plaque in [St Paul's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul's,_Covent_Garden "St Paul's, Covent Garden"), [Covent Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covent_Garden "Covent Garden"), London commemorating Pepys as a witness to the first performance of the puppet show [Punch and Judy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_and_Judy "Punch and Judy") in 1662

The diary gives a detailed account of Pepys' personal life. He was fond of [wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine "Wine"), plays, and the company of other people. He also spent time evaluating his fortune and his place in the world. He was always curious and often acted on that curiosity, as he acted upon almost all his impulses. Periodically, he would resolve to devote more time to hard work instead of leisure. For example, in his entry for New Year's Eve, 1661, he writes: "I have newly taken a solemn oath about abstaining from plays and wine…" The following months reveal his lapses to the reader; by 17 February, it is recorded, "Here I drank wine upon necessity, being ill for the want of it."

Pepys was one of the most important civil servants of his age, and was also a widely cultivated man, taking an interest in books, music, the theatre, and science. Aside from English, he was fluent in French and read many texts in [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin"). His favourite author was [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil "Virgil"). He was passionately interested in music; he composed, sang, and played for pleasure, and even arranged music lessons for his servants. He played the [lute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lute "Lute"), [viol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viol "Viol"), [violin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin "Violin"), [flageolet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flageolet "Flageolet"), [recorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recorder_(musical_instrument) "Recorder (musical instrument)") and [spinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinet "Spinet") to varying degrees of proficiency.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) He was also a keen singer, performing at home, in coffee houses, and even in [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8) He and his wife took flageolet lessons from master [Thomas Greeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Greeting "Thomas Greeting").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-42) He also taught his wife to sing and paid for dancing lessons for her (although these stopped when he became jealous of the dancing master).

Pepys was an investor in the [Company of Royal Adventurers Trading to Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_African_Company "Royal African Company"), which held the Royal monopoly on trading along the [west coast of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa") in [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold"), [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver "Silver"), [ivory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory "Ivory") and [slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade "Atlantic slave trade").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParker2011126-43)

#### Sexual relations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Sexual relations")]

Propriety did not prevent him from engaging in a number of extramarital liaisons with various women that were chronicled in his diary, often in some detail when relating the intimate details. The most dramatic of these encounters was with [Deborah Willet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deb_Willet "Deb Willet"), a young woman engaged as a [companion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady's_companion "Lady's companion") for Elisabeth Pepys. On 25 October 1668, Pepys was surprised by his wife as he embraced Deb Willet; he writes that his wife "coming up suddenly, did find me imbracing the girl con _[with]_ my hand sub _[under]_ su _[her]_ coats; and endeed I was with my main _[hand]_ in her cunny. I was at a wonderful loss upon it and the girl also...." Following this event, he was characteristically filled with remorse, but (equally characteristically) continued to pursue Willet after she had been dismissed from the Pepys household.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-44) Pepys also had a habit of fondling the breasts of his maid Mary Mercer while she dressed him in the morning.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryson2010123-45)

Pepys may also have dallied with a leading actress of the Restoration period, [Mary Knep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Knep "Mary Knep"). "Mrs Knep was the wife of a [Smithfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithfield,_London "Smithfield, London") horsedealer, and the mistress of Pepys"—or at least "she granted him a share of her favours".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTECunningham190812,_171-46) Scholars disagree on the full extent of the Pepys/Knep relationship, but much of later generations' knowledge of Knep comes from the diary. Pepys first met Knep on 6 December 1665. He described her as "pretty enough, but the most excellent, mad-humoured thing, and sings the noblest that I ever heard in my life." He called her husband "an ill, melancholy, jealous-looking fellow"[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-47) and suspected him of abusing his wife. Knep provided Pepys with backstage access and was a conduit for theatrical and social gossip. When they wrote notes to each other, Pepys signed himself "Dapper Dickey", while Knep was "[Barbry Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Allen_(song) "Barbara Allen (song)")" (a popular song that was an item in her musical repertory). Pepys' reference to purchasing the pornographic book _[L'Escole des Filles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Escole\_des\_Filles "L'Escole des Filles")_ appears to be the first English reference to pornography. He writes in his diary that it was a "mighty lewd book", and burned it after reading it.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoxen1963-48)

Much of Pepys' behaviour towards women, which he cataloged himself in his diary, would today be considered sexual harassment, sexual assault, and rape.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-Loveman-49) He wrote of using "force" or "great force" to achieve his sexual aims, sometimes causing injury to himself. He also described molesting women in their sleep.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-50) Despite his kindness and emotional loyalty towards some women in his life, Pepys ultimately believed men were entitled to the bodies of girls and women. Kate Loveman of Cambridge University describes this belief: "[In his diary] Pepys's sexual language of being 'kind', 'touching', and 'tumbling' emphasized his indulgence and playfulness, while masking coercion and violence; meanwhile, [his victim] Lane's claims of assault he regarded as exemplifying a woman's 'falseness', not because he thought there had been no violence, but because she had no moral right to protest."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-Loveman-49)

### Text of the diary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Text of the diary")]

The diary was written in one of the many standard forms of [shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shorthand "Shorthand") used in Pepys' time, in this case called [tachygraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Shelton_(stenographer)#Shelton's_shorthand "Thomas Shelton (stenographer)"), and devised by [Thomas Shelton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Shelton_(stenographer) "Thomas Shelton (stenographer)"). It is clear from its content that it was written as a purely personal record of his life and not for publication, yet there are indications that Pepys took steps to preserve the bound manuscripts of his diary. He wrote it out in fair copy from rough notes, and he also had the loose pages bound into six volumes, catalogued them in his library with all his other books, and is likely to have suspected that eventually someone would find them interesting.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-51)

## After the diary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: After the diary")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Samuel_Pepys_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller_1689.jpg/250px-Samuel_Pepys_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller_1689.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Pepys_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller_1689.jpg)

Samuel Pepys painted by [Sir Godfrey Kneller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_Kneller "Godfrey Kneller") in 1689

Pepys' health suffered from the long hours that he worked throughout the period of the diary. Specifically, he believed that his eyesight had been affected by his work.[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-54) He reluctantly concluded in his last entry, dated 31 May 1669, that he should completely stop writing for the sake of his eyes, and only dictate to his clerks from then on,[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-55) which meant that he could no longer keep his diary.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-56)

Pepys and his wife took a holiday to France and the [Low Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries") in June–October 1669; on their return, Elisabeth fell ill and died on 10 November 1669. Pepys erected a monument to her in the church of St Olave's, Hart Street, London. Pepys never remarried, but he did have a long-term housekeeper named Mary Skinner who was assumed by many of his contemporaries to be his mistress and sometimes referred to as Mrs. Pepys. In his will, he left her an [annuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_annuity "Life annuity") of £200 and many of his possessions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

### Member of Parliament and Secretary of the Admiralty

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Member of Parliament and Secretary of the Admiralty")]
