## After the diary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: After the diary")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Samuel_Pepys_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller_1689.jpg/250px-Samuel_Pepys_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller_1689.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Pepys_by_Sir_Godfrey_Kneller_1689.jpg)

Samuel Pepys painted by [Sir Godfrey Kneller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_Kneller "Godfrey Kneller") in 1689

Pepys' health suffered from the long hours that he worked throughout the period of the diary. Specifically, he believed that his eyesight had been affected by his work.[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-54) He reluctantly concluded in his last entry, dated 31 May 1669, that he should completely stop writing for the sake of his eyes, and only dictate to his clerks from then on,[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-55) which meant that he could no longer keep his diary.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-56)

Pepys and his wife took a holiday to France and the [Low Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries") in June–October 1669; on their return, Elisabeth fell ill and died on 10 November 1669. Pepys erected a monument to her in the church of St Olave's, Hart Street, London. Pepys never remarried, but he did have a long-term housekeeper named Mary Skinner who was assumed by many of his contemporaries to be his mistress and sometimes referred to as Mrs. Pepys. In his will, he left her an [annuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_annuity "Life annuity") of £200 and many of his possessions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnighton2004-8)

### Member of Parliament and Secretary of the Admiralty

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Member of Parliament and Secretary of the Admiralty")]

[![Image 19: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(May 2017)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

In 1672, he became an Elder Brother of Trinity House and served in this capacity until 1689; he was Master of Trinity House in 1676–1677 and again in 1685–1686.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenning1983226-57) In 1673, he was promoted to Secretary of the Admiralty Commission and elected MP for [Castle Rising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Rising_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Castle Rising (UK Parliament constituency)") in Norfolk.

In 1673, he was involved with the establishment of the [Royal Mathematical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Mathematical_School "Royal Mathematical School") at [Christ's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ's_Hospital "Christ's Hospital"), which was to train 40 boys annually in navigation, for the benefit of the Royal Navy and the English Merchant Navy. In 1675, he was appointed a Governor of Christ's Hospital and for many years he took a close interest in its affairs. Among his papers are two detailed memoranda on the administration of the school. In 1699, after the successful conclusion of a seven-year campaign to get the master of the Mathematical School replaced by a man who knew more about the sea, he was rewarded for his service as a Governor by being made a [Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City#Freedom_of_the_City_of_London "Freedom of the City") of the City of London. He also served as Master (without ever having been a Freeman or Liveryman) of the [Clothworkers' Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clothworkers'_Company "Clothworkers' Company") (1677–8).

At the beginning of 1679, Pepys was elected MP for [Harwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harwich_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Harwich (UK Parliament constituency)") in Charles II's third parliament which formed part of the [Cavalier Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier_Parliament "Cavalier Parliament"). He was elected along with [Sir Anthony Deane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Deane_(mayor) "Anthony Deane (mayor)"), a Harwich alderman and leading naval architect, to whom Pepys had been a patron since 1662. By May of that year, they were under attack from their political enemies. Pepys resigned as Secretary of the Admiralty. They were imprisoned in the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London "Tower of London") on suspicion of treasonable correspondence with France, specifically leaking naval intelligence. The charges are believed to have been fabricated under the direction of [Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Ashley-Cooper,_1st_Earl_of_Shaftesbury "Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-58) Pepys was accused, among other things, of being a secret member of the [Catholic Church in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_England "Catholic Church in England"). Pepys and Deane were released in July, but proceedings against them were not dropped until June 1680.

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Samuel_Pepys%2C_attributed_to_John_Riley.jpg/250px-Samuel_Pepys%2C_attributed_to_John_Riley.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Pepys_by_John_Closterman.jpg)

Pepys painted by [John Closterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Closterman "John Closterman") in the 1690s

Though he had resigned from the Tangier committee in 1679, in 1683 he was sent to Tangier to assist [Lord Dartmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Legge,_1st_Baron_Dartmouth "George Legge, 1st Baron Dartmouth") with the evacuation and abandonment of the English colony. After six months' service, he travelled back through Spain accompanied by the naval engineer [Edmund Dummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Dummer_(naval_engineer) "Edmund Dummer (naval engineer)"), returning to England after a particularly rough passage on 30 March 1684.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-59) In June 1684, once more in favour, he was appointed King's Secretary for the affairs of the Admiralty, a post that he retained after the death of Charles II (February 1685) and the accession of [James II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England"). The phantom [Pepys Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepys_Island "Pepys Island"), alleged to be near [South Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Georgia_Island "South Georgia Island"), was named after him in 1684, having been first "discovered" during his tenure at the Admiralty.

From 1685 to 1688, he was active not only as Secretary of the Admiralty, but also as MP for Harwich. He had been elected MP for [Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandwich_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Sandwich (UK Parliament constituency)"), but this election was contested and he immediately withdrew to Harwich. When James fled the country at the end of 1688, Pepys's career also came to an end. In January 1689, he was defeated in the parliamentary election at Harwich; in February, one week after the accession of [William III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_England "William III of England") and [Mary II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_II "Mary II"), he resigned his secretaryship.

### Royal Society

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Royal Society")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/NewtonsPrincipia.jpg/250px-NewtonsPrincipia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NewtonsPrincipia.jpg)

[Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton")'s personal copy of the first edition of his _Principia Mathematica_, with the imprimatur in Pepys's name

He was elected a Fellow of the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society "Royal Society") in 1665 and served as its President from 1 December 1684 to 30 November 1686. [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton")'s _[Principia Mathematica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophi%C3%A6\_Naturalis\_Principia\_Mathematica "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica")_ was published during this period, and the [imprimatur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imprimatur "Imprimatur") on the book's title page is signed by Pepys in his role as president. There is a [probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability "Probability") problem called the "[Newton–Pepys problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%E2%80%93Pepys_problem "Newton–Pepys problem")" that arose out of correspondence between Newton and Pepys about whether one is more likely to roll at least one six with six dice or at least two sixes with twelve dice.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-60) It has only recently been noted that the gambling advice that Newton gave Pepys was correct, while the logical argument with which Newton accompanied it was unsound.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStigler2006-61)

### Retirement and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Retirement and death")]

He was imprisoned on suspicion of [Jacobitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobitism "Jacobitism") from May to July 1689 and again in June 1690, but no charges were ever successfully brought against him. After his release, he retired from public life at age 57. He moved out of London ten years later (1701) to a house in [Clapham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapham "Clapham") owned by his friend [William Hewer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hewer "William Hewer"), who had begun his career working for Pepys in the admiralty.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-62) Clapham was in the country at the time; it is now part of inner London.

Pepys lived there until his death on 26 May 1703. He had no children and bequeathed his estate to his unmarried nephew John Jackson. Pepys had disinherited his nephew Samuel Jackson for marrying contrary to his wishes. When John Jackson died in 1724, Pepys' estate reverted to Anne, daughter of Archdeacon Samuel Edgeley, niece of Will Hewer and sister of Hewer Edgeley, nephew and godson of Pepys' old Admiralty employee and friend Will Hewer. Hewer was also childless and left his immense estate to his nephew Hewer Edgeley (consisting mostly of the Clapham property, as well as lands in Clapham, London, Westminster, and Norfolk) on condition that the nephew (and godson) would adopt the surname Hewer. So Will Hewer's heir became Hewer Edgeley-Hewer, and he adopted the old Will Hewer home in Clapham as his residence. That is how the Edgeley family acquired the estates of both Samuel Pepys and Will Hewer, with sister Anne inheriting Pepys' estate, and brother Hewer inheriting that of Will Hewer. On the death of Hewer Edgeley-Hewer in 1728, the old Hewer estate went to Edgeley-Hewer's widow Elizabeth, who left the 432-acre (175-hectare) estate to Levett Blackborne, the son of Abraham Blackborne, merchant of Clapham, and other family members, who later sold it off in lots. Lincoln's Inn barrister Levett Blackborne also later acted as attorney in legal scuffles for the heirs who had inherited the Pepys estate.

Pepys' former [protégé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prot%C3%A9g%C3%A9 "Protégé") and friend Hewer acted as the executor of Pepys's estate.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-63)

Pepys was buried along with his wife in [St Olave's Church, Hart Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Olave's_Church,_Hart_Street "St Olave's Church, Hart Street") in London.

## Pepys Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Pepys Library")]

Main article: [Pepys Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepys_Library "Pepys Library")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/PepysLibraryCambridge.jpg/250px-PepysLibraryCambridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PepysLibraryCambridge.jpg)

The [Pepys Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepys_Library "Pepys Library") of [Magdalene College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalene_College,_Cambridge "Magdalene College, Cambridge")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Pepys_Library_c1870.jpg/250px-Pepys_Library_c1870.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pepys_Library_c1870.jpg)

Pepys Library c.1870

Pepys was a lifelong [bibliophile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliophile "Bibliophile") and carefully nurtured his large collection of books, manuscripts, and prints. At his death, there were more than 3,000 volumes, including the diary, all carefully catalogued and indexed; they form one of the most important surviving 17th-century private [libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library "Library"). The most important items in the Library are the six original bound manuscripts of Pepys' diary, but there are other remarkable holdings, including:[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-64)

*   [Incunabula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incunabula "Incunabula") by [William Caxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Caxton "William Caxton"), [Wynkyn de Worde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynkyn_de_Worde "Wynkyn de Worde") and [Richard Pynson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Pynson "Richard Pynson")
*   Sixty medieval manuscripts
*   The _[Pepys Manuscript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepys\_Manuscript "Pepys Manuscript")_, a late-15th-century English [choirbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choirbook "Choirbook")
*   Naval records such as two of the '[Anthony Rolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Roll "Anthony Roll")', illustrating the Royal Navy's ships c.1546, including the _[Mary Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary\_Rose "Mary Rose")_
*   [Sir Francis Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Francis_Drake "Sir Francis Drake")'s personal [almanac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almanac "Almanac")
*   Over 1,800 printed [ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballad "Ballad"), one of the finest collections in existence.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-65)

The library includes an extensive collection of documents relating to the administration of the navy in Pepys' time. These have been used as a dominant source for understanding how the navy was governed and the level of influence exerted by those involved. Comparison of notes made by Pepys' brother John of a meeting on 22 July 1676 with the official minutes taken by Samuel calls into question the completeness and accuracy of the latter. For instance, the official minutes make no mention that the [Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England") even attended, when John's notes make clear that the Duke was an active participant. The suggestion is made that Samuel Pepys' naval journal presents a "flawed and incomplete picture" of how the navy was run in the 1670s, despite it being a key source, widely cited by historians.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies2017257%E2%80%93261-66)

Pepys made detailed provisions in his will for the preservation of his book collection. His nephew and heir John Jackson died in 1723, when it was transferred intact to Magdalene College, Cambridge, where it can be seen in the [Pepys Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepys_Library "Pepys Library"). The bequest included all the original bookcases and his elaborate instructions that placement of the books "be strictly reviewed and, where found requiring it, more nicely adjusted".

The Ephemera Society emblem uses Pepys' portrait and characterizes him as "the first general ephemerist."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-67) Two large albums of [ephemera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephemera "Ephemera") saved by Pepys are in his library.

## Publication history of the diary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Publication history of the diary")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Samuel_Pepys_diary_manuscript_volumes.jpg/500px-Samuel_Pepys_diary_manuscript_volumes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Pepys_diary_manuscript_volumes.jpg)

The six volumes of the diary manuscript

Motivated by the publication of [John Evelyn's Diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Evelyn's_Diary "John Evelyn's Diary") in 1818, [Lord Granville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granville_Leveson-Gower,_1st_Earl_Granville "Granville Leveson-Gower, 1st Earl Granville") deciphered a few pages.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHammerton1937-68)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_][John Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Smith_(Anglican_priest) "John Smith (Anglican priest)") (later the [Rector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rector_(ecclesiastical) "Rector (ecclesiastical)") of [St Mary the Virgin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_St_Mary_the_Virgin,_Baldock "Church of St Mary the Virgin, Baldock") in [Baldock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldock "Baldock")) was then engaged to transcribe the diaries into plain English. He laboured at this task for three years, from 1819 to 1822, unaware until nearly finished that a key to the shorthand system was stored in Pepys' library a few shelves above the diary volumes. Others had apparently succeeded in reading the diary earlier, perhaps knowing about the key, because a work of 1812 quotes from a passage of it.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBryson2010211%E2%80%93212-69) Smith's transcription, which is also kept in the Pepys Library, was the basis for the first published edition of the diary, edited by [Lord Braybrooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Griffin,_3rd_Baron_Braybrooke "Richard Griffin, 3rd Baron Braybrooke"), released in two volumes in 1825 along with selected correspondence. The second edition was brought out in 1828. An enlarged third edition was published in 1848. The fourth edition was published in 1854.

A second transcription, done with the benefit of the key but often less accurately, was completed in 1875 by [Mynors Bright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mynors_Bright "Mynors Bright") and published in 1875–1879.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-70) This added about a third to the previously published text, but still left only about 80% of the diary in print.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWheatley1893Prefacs-71)[Henry B. Wheatley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_B._Wheatley "Henry B. Wheatley"), drawing on both his predecessors, produced a new edition in 1893–1899,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWheatley1893-72) revised in 1926 with extensive notes and an index.

All of these editions omitted passages (chiefly about Pepys' sexual adventures) that the editors thought were too obscene ever to be printed. Wheatley, in the preface to his edition, noted, "a few passages which cannot possibly be printed. It may be thought by some that these omissions are due to an unnecessary squeamishness, but it is not really so, and readers are therefore asked to have faith in the judgement of the editor." Wheatley claims to have indicated all such omissions with an ellipsis, but comparison with the modern text indicates that he did not always do this, and that he silently bowdlerised a number of words.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-73)

The complete, unexpurgated, and definitive edition, edited and transcribed by [Robert Latham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Latham_(editor) "Robert Latham (editor)") and William Matthews, was published by Bell & Hyman, London, and the [University of California Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California_Press "University of California Press"), Berkeley, in nine volumes, along with separate Companion and Index volumes, over the years 1970–1983. Various single-volume abridgements of this text are also available.

The Introduction in Volume I provides a scholarly but readable account of "The Diarist", "The Diary" ("The Manuscript", "The Shorthand", and "The Text"), "History of Previous Editions", "The Diary as Literature", and "The Diary as History". The Companion provides a long series of detailed essays about Pepys and his world.

The first unabridged recording of the diary as an audiobook was published in 2015 by _Naxos AudioBooks_.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-74)

On 1 January 2003 Phil Gyford started a [weblog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weblog "Weblog"), pepysdiary.com, that serialised the diary one day each evening together with annotations from the public and experts alike. In December 2003 the blog won the best specialist blog award in _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_'s Best of British Blogs.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-75) In 2021, Gyford noted the existence of the Samuel Pepys [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") account; set up in 2008, the account similarly serialises Pepys' diary each day.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-76)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-77)

## Adaptations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Pepys&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Adaptations")]

In 1958, the BBC produced a serial called _[The Diary of Samuel Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Diary\_of\_Samuel\_Pepys "The Diary of Samuel Pepys")_, in which [Peter Sallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Sallis "Peter Sallis") played the title role. In 2003, a television film, _[The Private Life of Samuel Pepys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Private\_Life\_of\_Samuel\_Pepys "The Private Life of Samuel Pepys")_ aired on [BBC2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC2 "BBC2"), in which [Steve Coogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Coogan "Steve Coogan") played Pepys. The 2004 film _[Stage Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage\_Beauty "Stage Beauty")_ concerns London theatre in the 17th century and is based on [Jeffrey Hatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Hatcher "Jeffrey Hatcher")'s play _Compleat Female Stage Beauty_, which in turn was inspired by a reference in Pepys' diary to the actor [Edward Kynaston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Kynaston_(actor) "Edward Kynaston (actor)"), who played female roles in the days when women were forbidden to appear on stage. Pepys is a character in the film and is portrayed as an ardent devotee of the theatre. [Hugh Bonneville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Bonneville "Hugh Bonneville") plays Pepys. [Daniel Mays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Mays "Daniel Mays") portrays Pepys in _[The Great Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Great\_Fire\_(TV\_series) "The Great Fire (TV series)")_, a 2014 BBC television miniseries. [BBC Radio 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_4 "BBC Radio 4") has broadcast serialised radio dramatisations of the diary. In the 1990s it was performed as a _Classic Serial_ starring [Bill Nighy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Nighy "Bill Nighy"),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-78) and in the 2010s it was serialised as part of the _[Woman's Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman's\_Hour "Woman's Hour")_ radio magazine programme.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Pepys#cite_note-79) One audiobook edition of Pepys' diary selections is narrated by [Kenneth Branagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Branagh "Kenneth Branagh"). A fictionalised Pepys narrates the second chapter of [Harry Turtledove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Turtledove "Harry Turtledove")'s science fiction novel _[A Different Flesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Different\_Flesh "A Different Flesh")_ (serialised 1985–1988, book form 1988). **Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich** (27 July 1625 – 28 May 1672), was an English military officer, politician and diplomat from [Barnwell, Northamptonshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnwell,_Northamptonshire "Barnwell, Northamptonshire"). During the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") he served with the [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") army, and was a member of the [Parliament of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") at various times between 1645 and 1660. Under [the Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Protectorate "The Protectorate"), he was also a member of the [English Council of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Council_of_State "English Council of State") and [General at sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_at_sea "General at sea").

In the political infighting that followed the death of [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") in 1658, he played an important role in bringing about the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") in May 1660. Created [Earl of Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Sandwich "Earl of Sandwich") by [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), he served as [Ambassador to Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_Kingdom_of_England_to_Portugal "List of ambassadors of the Kingdom of England to Portugal") from 1661 to 1662. He was appointed [Ambassador to Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_Kingdom_to_Spain "List of ambassadors of the United Kingdom to Spain") in 1666 and helped to negotiate the [1667 Treaty of Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Madrid_(1667) "Treaty of Madrid (1667)").

When the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War") began in 1665, he commanded a naval [squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squadron_(naval) "Squadron (naval)") but was later suspended in a dispute over [prize money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_(law) "Prize (law)"). He was restored to command when the [Third Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Dutch_War "Third Anglo-Dutch War") began in May 1672, but was killed at the [Battle of Solebay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Solebay "Battle of Solebay") in June. Montagu is one of the best-known characters of the 1660s, being a central figure in the diaries of his distant cousin the naval official Samuel Pepys.

## Personal details

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal details")]

Edward Montagu was born on 25 July 1625 as the only surviving son of [Sir Sidney Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Montagu_(MP,_died_1644) "Sidney Montagu (MP, died 1644)") (c. 1572–1644) and his first wife, Paulina Pepys (died 1638), great-aunt of Samuel Pepys. On 7 November 1642 Edward married Jemimah Crew, daughter of [John Crew, 1st Baron Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Crew,_1st_Baron_Crew "John Crew, 1st Baron Crew"), and Jemima Waldegrave, whom Pepys in his diary refers to with great affection as "My Lady". The couple had ten children:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTELatham2000255-1)

*   Jemima (1646–1671)
*   [Edward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_2nd_Earl_of_Sandwich "Edward Montagu, 2nd Earl of Sandwich") (1648–1688)
*   Paulina (1649–1669)
*   [Sidney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Wortley_Montagu "Sidney Wortley Montagu") (1650–1727)
*   [Oliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Montagu "Oliver Montagu") (c. 1655–1689)
*   [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Montagu_(Trinity) "John Montagu (Trinity)") (c. 1655–1729)
*   [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Montagu_(died_1721) "Charles Montagu (died 1721)") (1658–1721)
*   Anne (1660–1729)
*   Catherine (1661–1757)
*   James (b. 1664)

Paulina's death in February 1669, aged only twenty, was a great source of grief to her father. Pepys, who called her "a peevish lady", called to pay his condolences, but found him "shut away for sorrow".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994248-2)

## First English Civil War and Interregnum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: First English Civil War and Interregnum")]

Although his father was a [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier"), when the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") began in August 1642, Montagu served in the [Eastern Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Association "Eastern Association") army led by his [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") cousin, [the Earl of Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_2nd_Earl_of_Manchester "Edward Montagu, 2nd Earl of Manchester"). He raised a regiment of infantry which during the 1644 campaign fought at [Marston Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marston_Moor "Battle of Marston Moor"), the [Siege of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_York "Siege of York") and [Second Newbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Newbury "Second Battle of Newbury"). Despite his family relationship, Montagu supported those in [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") who expressed dissatisfaction with the conduct of the war by Manchester and [Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Devereux,_3rd_Earl_of_Essex "Robert Devereux, 3rd Earl of Essex").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTECotton1975212-3)

This resulted in the creation of the [New Model Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Model_Army "New Model Army") in February 1645 and the passing of the [Self-denying Ordinance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-denying_Ordinance "Self-denying Ordinance"), requiring those holding military commissions to resign from Parliament. As members of the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords"), Manchester and Essex were automatically removed, since unlike MPs they could not resign their titles.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood1958398%E2%80%93399-4) Montagu's regiment was incorporated into the New Model, taking part in the June 1645 [Battle of Naseby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Naseby "Battle of Naseby"), followed by the [capture of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Bristol_(1645) "Siege of Bristol (1645)"). In October he resigned from the army as required by the Ordinance when was appointed MP for [Huntingdonshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huntingdonshire_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Huntingdonshire (UK Parliament constituency)"), a seat formerly held by his father who died in September 1644.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHealy2010-5)

Montagu played no part in the [Second English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_English_Civil_War "Second English Civil War") and retired from Parliament after [Pride's Purge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride's_Purge "Pride's Purge") in December 1648 to live quietly at home. He returned to politics in 1653 when his neighbour [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") nominated him to the [Barebones Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barebones_Parliament "Barebones Parliament") as MP for Huntingdonshire, a seat formerly held by his father who died in September 1644.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHealy2010-5) He was also appointed to the [English Council of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Council_of_State "English Council of State"), an office he held until it was dissolved in 1659, and was re-elected to the [First Protectorate Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Protectorate_Parliament "First Protectorate Parliament") in 1654, then the [Second Protectorate Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Protectorate_Parliament "Second Protectorate Parliament") in 1656.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHenning1983-6)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Edward_Montagu.jpeg/250px-Edward_Montagu.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Montagu.jpeg)

Portrait of Sandwich by Sir [Peter Lely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Lely "Peter Lely"), painted 1666, part of the [Flagmen of Lowestoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagmen_of_Lowestoft "Flagmen of Lowestoft") series.

During the [Anglo-Spanish War (1654–1660)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Spanish_War_(1654%E2%80%931660) "Anglo-Spanish War (1654–1660)"), he was appointed joint [General at Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_at_Sea "General at Sea") with [Robert Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blake_(admiral) "Robert Blake (admiral)"), taking part in an expedition into the [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean "Mediterranean"). This experience made him a leading advocate of establishing a British naval base in the region, an ambition realised with the acquisition of [English Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Tangier "English Tangier") in 1661.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTECorbett190411-7) In February 1657, he was one of the so-called "New Cromwellians" who supported the [Humble Petition and Advice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humble_Petition_and_Advice "Humble Petition and Advice"), inviting Cromwell to declare himself king and advocating the re-establishment of a national church. The measure was opposed by army radicals including [Charles Fleetwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Fleetwood "Charles Fleetwood") and [John Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambert_(general) "John Lambert (general)") and ultimately rejected.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatterall190336%E2%80%9337-8)

In June 1658 he commanded the naval squadron that blockaded [Dunkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Dunkirk_(1658) "Siege of Dunkirk (1658)") and when Cromwell died in September, Montagu remained loyal to his son and appointed successor [Richard Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). During his brief and disastrous rule as [Lord Protector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Protector "Lord Protector"), Montagu remained at sea and in early 1659 was sent to mediate between Sweden and Denmark; however, he was suspected of secret communication with the exiled [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") and the republicans [Algernon Sidney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Sidney "Algernon Sidney") and [Sir Robert Honywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Honywood_(New_Romney_MP) "Robert Honywood (New Romney MP)") were sent to monitor his activity.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard199462-9) He was recalled and investigated by the newly installed [Rump Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rump_Parliament "Rump Parliament"); although no evidence was found, he was dismissed from command.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies2004-10)

## Restoration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Restoration")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam%2C_may_24_1660_%28Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier%2C_1665%29.jpg/500px-The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam%2C_may_24_1660_%28Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier%2C_1665%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_arrival_of_King_Charles_II_of_England_in_Rotterdam,_may_24_1660_(Lieve_Pietersz._Verschuier,_1665).jpg)

Charles leaves the Dutch Republic for England, 24 May 1660

By the end of 1659 England appeared to be drifting into [anarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchy "Anarchy"), with widespread demands for new elections and an end to military rule. In February 1660, [George Monck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Monck,_1st_Duke_of_Albemarle "George Monck, 1st Duke of Albemarle"), military commander in Scotland, marched into London and declared his support for the Rump against the Republican faction led by [John Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambert_(general) "John Lambert (general)"). Montagu resumed command of the navy and was returned as MP for the important port of [Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Dover (UK Parliament constituency)") when elections were held for a [Convention Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_Parliament_(1660) "Convention Parliament (1660)") in April.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris191243%E2%80%9344-11)

This placed him in a powerful position during negotiations for the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration"); when Parliament resolved to proclaim Charles king and invited him to return to England, Montagu commanded the fleet that brought him from the [Dutch Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Republic "Dutch Republic") on 24 May.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton1989131-12) Two months later, on 12 July 1660, he was created **Baron Montagu of St Neots**, **Viscount Hinchingbrooke**, and **Earl of Sandwich**. King Charles also made him a [Knight of the Garter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Garter "Order of the Garter") and appointed him [Master of the Great Wardrobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_the_Great_Wardrobe "Master of the Great Wardrobe"), [Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiral "Admiral") of the narrow seas (the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel") and southern [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea")), and [Lieutenant Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Admiral "Lieutenant Admiral") to [The Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England"), [Lord High Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Admiralty "British Admiralty") of England. He carried [St. Edward's staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sceptre_with_the_Cross "Sceptre with the Cross") at Charles' subsequent coronation. [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon"), who liked and admired Sandwich, wrote that the conferring of these honours caused much resentment among those Royalists who had gone into exile with their King, and regarded Sandwich as a "diehard" Cromwellian; yet adds that his charm of manner made it almost impossible to dislike him.

He was appointed [Ambassador to Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_Kingdom_of_England_to_Portugal "List of ambassadors of the Kingdom of England to Portugal") in 1661, and strongly favoured the Portuguese marriage, through which England obtained [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay "Bombay") and [Tangier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Tangier "English Tangier"). Sandwich, like others, saw a great future for Tangier as an international trade centre, and he commanded the fleet which took possession of the city in January 1662, purchasing a house there. Returning to England, in his capacity as Ambassador, he escorted the new Queen, [Catherine of Braganza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_of_Braganza "Catherine of Braganza"), from [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994109-13)

Montagu was a signatory to _The Several Declarations of The Company of Royal Adventurers of England Trading into Africa_, a document published in 1667 which led to the expansion of the [Royal Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_African_Company "Royal African Company").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-auto-16)

## The Prize Goods Scandal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The Prize Goods Scandal")]

In the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War") of 1665 to 1667 he fought at the [Battle of Lowestoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lowestoft "Battle of Lowestoft"), an English victory, but defeat at the [Battle of Vågen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_V%C3%A5gen "Battle of Vågen") led to him being removed from active service. His reputation suffered another serious blow when he failed to prevent his sailors from plundering a number of Dutch [VOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company")[prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_(law) "Prize (law)") ships, loaded with precious spices from the [East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Indies "East Indies"), which he had brought in. By long-standing custom the sailors could take any goods they found between the decks, but they were strictly forbidden to "break the bulk" i.e. ransack the ship's hold; yet this is just what Sandwich, an easy-going man with a notoriously poor understanding of money matters, permitted. When this became widely known, the rumour spread that Sandwich had unlawfully helped himself to a fortune (in fact he seems to have taken less than he was entitled to), and the public, who were still enduring the horrors of the [Great Plague of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London"), reacted with such unexpected fury that a minor mishap became a national affair: "the Prize Goods Scandal". Although Clarendon wrote that Sandwich was too likeable to have any personal enemies, he did have political opponents, including his own superior at the Admiralty, [James, Duke of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England"), and James' influential secretary [Sir William Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Coventry "William Coventry"), who were happy to exploit the scandal. He felt obliged to obtain a [royal pardon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_pardon "Royal pardon"): the King, mindful of his good services at the Restoration, willingly granted it.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994140%E2%80%93142-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-auto-16)

## Ambassador to Spain

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Ambassador to Spain")]

During his absence from battle, Sandwich served as England's ambassador to Spain, replacing [Sir Richard Fanshawe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Richard_Fanshawe,_1st_Baronet "Sir Richard Fanshawe, 1st Baronet"). This is further evidence that despite his unpopularity, he retained the King's confidence, although his political fortunes, like those of his friend and patron Clarendon, were in decline. Sandwich himself had told Pepys the previous year not to put too much reliance on the friendship of any "great man". After the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London") Sandwich downplayed the damage to the Spanish King, claiming that London's slums were the only thing in ashes. This slant on the events was also practised by England's ambassadors throughout Europe.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-18)

As Ambassador his most notable achievement was the [Anglo-Spanish Commercial Treaty of 1667](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Madrid_(1667) "Treaty of Madrid (1667)"), which laid the foundations for a prosperous trading relationship between the two countries which lasted for over a century.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-19) He also acted as mediator in the peace negotiations between Spain and Portugal which resulted in the [Treaty of Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lisbon_(1668) "Treaty of Lisbon (1668)"). Like all Ambassadors of the era, he found the cost of running an embassy ruinous (he had never had a good head for business) and on his return to England in the autumn of 1668 one of his first actions was to borrow money from his cousin Samuel Pepys.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-20) On his way back from Spain, he again visited Tangier to report on the condition of the garrison there.

In 1670 he escorted the King's sister [Henrietta of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta_of_England "Henrietta of England"), [Duchess of Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchess_of_Orleans "Duchess of Orleans"), from France to England to negotiate the [Secret Treaty of Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_Treaty_of_Dover "Secret Treaty of Dover") between her brother and [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV"). Of the existence of the Treaty's secret clauses, notably that by which Charles II pledged to convert to the [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") faith, Sandwich, like the general public, was quite unaware.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994253%E2%80%934-21) In the same year he was appointed President of the Privy Council Committee on Foreign Plantations; he had always had a keen interest in international trade, despite his notorious inability to keep his own finances in order.

## Last campaign and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Last campaign and death")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Edward_Montagu%2C_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg/250px-Edward_Montagu%2C_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich_by_Sir_Peter_Lely.jpg)

Montagu in the 1660s

He was subsequently reappointed to a naval command, and by 1672 at the start of the [Third Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Dutch_War "Third Anglo-Dutch War"), he was Vice-Admiral of the Blue with the [_Royal James_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Royal_James "HMS Royal James") as his flagship. At the [Battle of Solebay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Solebay "Battle of Solebay") on 28 May, his ship was attacked by a group of [fire ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_ships "Fire ships") and was destroyed with the loss of many lives, including Sandwich himself. His body was washed ashore a week later, recognisable only from his clothing; it was unmarked and he appeared to have drowned.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies2004-10) Sandwich opposed the war and is said to have predicted his own death. Certainly, he told his friend [John Evelyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Evelyn "John Evelyn"), just before he sailed, that "he would see him no more".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994256-22)

On Wednesday 3 July 1672 he was buried in [Westminster Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey") after a [state funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_funeral "State funeral") that started with a procession along the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames") of five decorated barges from [Deptford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deptford "Deptford"). His body was landed at [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster") at about 5 pm and carried to the Abbey in a grand procession.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994262%E2%80%933-23)

## Sandwich and Samuel Pepys

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Sandwich and Samuel Pepys")]

Sandwich on his mother's side was the first cousin of John Pepys, the father of Samuel Pepys. Pepys started his career as a minor member of the Sandwich household and owed his appointments first to the Wardrobe and then as Clerk of the Acts to the [Navy Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navy_Board "Navy Board") to Sandwich's influence. Pepys' diary provides a detailed [primary source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_source "Primary source") of Sandwich's career in the 1660s.

They had a serious quarrel in 1663, when Pepys reprimanded Sandwich for living openly with his mistress, Elizabeth Becke, at her "mean house" in [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea,_London "Chelsea, London").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOllard1994116%E2%80%937-24) Pepys was concerned at the damage to their family's reputation, Sandwich's neglect of his official duties (thus risking the loss of any remaining influence he had at Court) and also at the insult to Sandwich's wife, to whom Pepys was deeply attached. Following a brief estrangement, friendly relations were resumed, although the two men were probably never as close again as they had been (Pepys, for example, is not mentioned in Sandwich's last will). For Pepys to raise the issue at all took considerable courage, considering how much he owed to his patron, and his Diary shows that he was strongly tempted to let the matter lie. Even when he did raise it he chose to write rather than confront Sandwich face to face.

In 1668 Pepys was somewhat perturbed when his wife [Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Pepys "Elisabeth Pepys"), during one of the violent quarrels which followed the discovery of his affair with her companion [Deb Willet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deb_Willet "Deb Willet"), told him that Sandwich had asked her to be his mistress.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-25) Since Pepys was in no doubt that she had refused, he decided to treat the matter as being closed, and friendly relations continued: Sandwich dined at their house for the first time a few months later.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-26) Pepys, on reflection, may have thought it possible that Elizabeth in her anger had invented the story to upset him, (as she undoubtedly invented the story that she was attending [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") services). Whatever their differences, Pepys in later life always remembered Sandwich, whom he called "that noble and unparalleled Lord", and his wife (who died in 1674) with affection and gratitude.

**Edward Montagu, 1st Earl of Sandwich** (27 July 1625 – 28 May 1672), was an English military officer, politician and diplomat from [Barnwell, Northamptonshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnwell,_Northamptonshire "Barnwell, Northamptonshire"). During the [First English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_English_Civil_War "First English Civil War") he served with the [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") army, and was a member of the [Parliament of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") at various times between 1645 and 1660. Under [the Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Protectorate "The Protectorate"), he was also a member of the [English Council of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Council_of_State "English Council of State") and [General at sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_at_sea "General at sea").

In the political infighting that followed the death of [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") in 1658, he played an important role in bringing about the [Stuart Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration") in May 1660. Created [Earl of Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Sandwich "Earl of Sandwich") by [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England"), he served as [Ambassador to Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_Kingdom_of_England_to_Portugal "List of ambassadors of the Kingdom of England to Portugal") from 1661 to 1662. He was appointed [Ambassador to Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_Kingdom_to_Spain "List of ambassadors of the United Kingdom to Spain") in 1666 and helped to negotiate the [1667 Treaty of Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Madrid_(1667) "Treaty of Madrid (1667)").

When the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War") began in 1665, he commanded a naval [squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squadron_(naval) "Squadron (naval)") but was later suspended in a dispute over [prize money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_(law) "Prize (law)"). He was restored to command when the [Third Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Dutch_War "Third Anglo-Dutch War") began in May 1672, but was killed at the [Battle of Solebay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Solebay "Battle of Solebay") in June. Montagu is one of the best-known characters of the 1660s, being a central figure in the diaries of his distant cousin the naval official Samuel Pepys.

## Personal details

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal details")]

Edward Montagu was born on 25 July 1625 as the only surviving son of [Sir Sidney Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Montagu_(MP,_died_1644) "Sidney Montagu (MP, died 1644)") (c. 1572–1644) and his first wife, Paulina Pepys (died 1638), great-aunt of Samuel Pepys. On 7 November 1642 Edward married Jemimah Crew, daughter of [John Crew, 1st Baron Crew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Crew,_1st_Baron_Crew "John Crew, 1st Baron Crew"), and Jemima Waldegrave, whom Pepys in his diary refers to with great affection as "My Lady". The couple had ten children:[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_1st_Earl_of_Sandwich#cite_note-FOOTNOTELatham2000255-1)

*   Jemima (1646–1671)
*   [Edward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Montagu,_2nd_Earl_of_Sandwich "Edward Montagu, 2nd Earl of Sandwich") (1648–1688)
*   Paulina (1649–1669)
*   [Sidney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Wortley_Montagu "Sidney Wortley Montagu") (1650–1727)
*   [Oliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Montagu "Oliver Montagu") (c. 1655–1689)
*   [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Montagu_(Trinity) "John Montagu (Trinity)") (c. 1655–1729)
*   [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Montagu_(died_1721) "Charles Montagu (died 1721)") (1658–1721)
*   Anne (1660–1729)
*   Catherine (1661–1757)
*   James (b. 1664)
